In California v. Texas, 141 S. Ct. 2104 (2021), the Court relied on the 
causation prong to reject a group of states’ challenge to the constitutionality of 
the Affordable Care Act. The states claimed that minimum essential coverage 
requirements had saddled them with additional costs related to greater 
enrollment in state-funded insurance programs. The Court found that the 
states had not established that the ACA’s provisions, rather than the 
consumers’ attraction to the programs’ benefits, had increased enrollm Ants.
And in Texas v. Pennsylvania, 141 S. Ct. 1230 (Mem) (2020), the Court 
stated in a brief opinion that "Texas has not demonstrated a judicially 
cognizable interest in the manner in which another State conducts its 
elections.”
A counterexample may be the recent decision in Biden v. Nebraska, 143
S.Ct. 2355 (2023), where the Court found that Missouri had standing to 
challenge the Biden administration’s student debt relief order because the 
state-run Missouri Higher Education Loan Authority would suffer reduced 
revenues as a result of the order. Because MOHELA functioned as an 
instrumentahty of the state, "[t]he harm to MOHELA in the performance of its 
pubhc function is necessarily a direct injury to Missouri itself.” The dissenters 
believed that the failure of MOHELA itself to join in the suit meant that the 
harmed party was not before the Court and that the usual rules against 
allowing plaintiffs to pursue the rights of third parties should preclude state 
standing.
Plaintiff states rehed upon Massachusetts v. EPA in asserting sta-ndi-ng to 
challenge DHS enforcement guidelines as unlawfully lenient in United States 
V. Texas, 599 U.S. 670 (2023), but the five-Justice majority treated the states’ 
invocation of that precedent dismissively, saying it “does not control this case” 
because it “involved a challenge to the denial of a statutorily authorized 
petition for rulemaking, not a challenge to an exercise of the Executive’s 
enforcement discretion,” id. at 685 n.6. Three other justices, separately 
concurring in the judgment, suggested that special solicitude for the states was 
dead, and good riddance: the concept had not “played a meaningful role in this 
Court’s decisions” since 2007; “the Court says nothing about ‘special sohcitude’ 
in [the present] case”; and “it’s hard not to think * * * that lower courts should 
just leave that idea on the shelf in future ones.” Id. at 688—89.
